card.p: Why your best work is waiting behind a rule you haven't written yet

card.h1: In 1960, a publisher bet Dr. Seuss fifty dollars

ul.li: Bennett Cerf of Random House wagered $50 that Theodor Geisel could not write a book using 50 different words or fewer
Geisel took the bet and agonized over it. The result was Green Eggs and Ham, published 12 August 1960
Forty-nine of its words are monosyllables; the single exception is "anywhere"
By some estimates it has sold north of 200 million copies — his best-selling book ever

card.p: Nobody remembers the books he wrote with unlimited vocabulary.

card.h1: And yet we hand people a blank page and call it a gift

ul.li: The default brief in most studios: open scope, open budget, "surprise us," no fixed deliverable
We treat every limit as damage — the client who won't move, the format that won't stretch, the palette we inherited
The thing we call creative freedom is often just an unmade decision handed downstream

card.p: I want to argue the opposite for the next twenty minutes: the constraint is not the obstacle to the work. It is the instrument.

ul.li: A 2022 meta-analysis in the Journal of Organizational Behavior pooled 111 published and unpublished studies on constraints and creative performance
It found a significant positive relationship between constraints and creativity
The surprise inside the surprise: the type of constraint mattered less than researchers assumed. Much of the older disagreement traced to methodology, not to the constraints themselves

card.p: The field spent years arguing about which constraints help. The answer looks more like: the boundary itself is doing the work.

card.h1: The finding that should annoy you most

ul.li: A Stanford study had participants design graphic advertisements, introducing a narrowing constraint — a specified target audience and ad size — at the beginning, middle, or end of prototyping
Prevailing wisdom says late requirement changes wreck the outcome. Late constraints produced the most novel results.
A second experiment induced design fixation — the thing we train people out of. Higher fixation also yielded more novel results

card.p: The 11th-hour scope change you dread may be the most generative event in the project.

card.h1: Harder was better, even when it was worse

ul.li: In a 2023 Creativity Research Journal study, participants wrote short sentences under low or high constraint on the initial letters they could use
Under high constraint they were less likely to succeed at all — but the sentences they did produce were judged more creative

card.p: That is the honest trade. Tight rules lower your hit rate and raise your ceiling. Plan for more failed attempts, not fewer.

card.h1: But constraint is a dose, not a virtue

ul.li: Organizational research proposes that multiple dimensions of constraint — on the problem and on the resources — have to be read together, not one at a time
Too little on both: ambiguous opportunity. Nobody knows what the work is, so nothing gets made
Too much on both: futile effort. Everyone knows what the work is and nobody can reach it
Balanced: intrinsic motivation and creative search both stay switched on

card.p: So the skill is not adding limits. It is tuning them.

card.h1: Two kinds of rules, and only one of them helps

ul.li: Constraints do two different jobs: exclusionary — ruling options out — and focusing — pointing attention at a region of the problem
"No stock photography" is exclusionary. It clears the table but tells you nothing
"Every image has to be something a customer could have shot on their own phone" excludes the same options and aims you somewhere

card.p: Test for the difference: read your rule aloud. If it only ends arguments, rewrite it until it also starts one.

card.h1: Filmmakers wrote theirs down and signed it

ul.li: On 13 March 1995 in Copenhagen, Lars von Trier and Thomas Vinterberg published the Dogme 95 manifesto and its ten-rule "Vow of Chastity"
Shoot on location. No sound produced apart from the images. Camera handheld. No optical work or filters. No superficial action. The film takes place here and now. The director must not be credited.
Their reasoning was explicit: "Discipline is the answer... we must put our films into uniform"

card.p: Note what the vow refuses to specify: the story. Every rule governs method. None governs meaning.

card.h1: Four steps, and you can run this on Monday

ol.li: Name the default. Write the version of this project any competent studio would make. That description is the thing you are trying to escape
Find the load-bearing freedom. Which single permission makes the default possible? Usually budget, stock imagery, or an unlimited palette
Remove it, and aim the hole. Convert the removal into a focusing rule — what you must now do, not just what you can't
Set the dose and the escape clause. Three to five rules. Write down in advance the one condition under which you'd break them

card.p: Five rules is a vow. Fifteen is a specification, and specifications produce compliance.

card.h1: Worked example: a salon rebrand that does not exist
card.p: This example is invented for this talk. Fenwick & Pike is a fictional salon; no client commissioned it, no work was delivered, and the visuals here are concept imagery, not case-study results.

ul.li: The default: soft neutral palette, serif wordmark, close-cropped model portraits, one script accent. Roughly every salon identity of the last decade
The load-bearing freedom: photography of people. Remove it and the whole default collapses

card.p: The vow: one typeface at two weights · two inks, no gradients · no photographs of people · every asset must survive reproduction at 30mm on a sticker.

ul.li: No people pushed the identity toward the objects of the trade — comb teeth, foil, the curve of a shear — as flat graphic marks
Two inks killed the soft gradient look and produced a hard, high-contrast system that survives a photocopier and a neon sign equally
The 30mm sticker rule was the load-bearer. It vetoed the delicate wordmark on week one, which is exactly what a good constraint does early
One typeface moved all the hierarchy into scale and spacing, which is cheaper to maintain and harder to get wrong

card.p: None of these were decisions. They were consequences. That is the point.

card.h1: How to tell your vow is wrong

ul.li: It only says no. A vow of pure prohibition is a filter, not a brief. Rewrite toward the focusing form
Nothing has died yet. If two weeks in nothing you liked has been vetoed, the rules are decorative
It has started governing meaning. Method rules are generative; rules about what the work may say are censorship in a better outfit
Everyone is miserable and nothing ships. That is futile effort, and the fix is to loosen one dimension, not to push harder

card.h1: Pick the freedom you're most afraid to lose
card.p: The evidence points one way: constraints predict better creative performance, late ones especially, and the real work is tuning the dose rather than defending your options.
So go back to the project sitting open on your desk. Find the permission you would defend hardest in a meeting. Take it away for two weeks and write down what happens.
Bennett Cerf's fifty dollars bought the best-selling thing Geisel ever made. Your version costs less than that.
